Procter & Gamble (PG -2.12%) just had its best day in more than six years, with the stock jumping 5.6% on Thursday after the company delivered a surprisingly strong fiscal first quarter in a challenging environment.
During a time when many of its customers are struggling with inflation and a high cost of living, the household products giant reported 4% organic sales growth. That performance also represents a significant bounce from flat organic sales growth in the previous quarter, which helps explain why the stock had its best day since the market started soaring in the recovery from the pandemic crash in March 2020.
Organic volume was up 2.4%, and the company delivered strong results in beauty, fabric, and home care. Overall revenue rose 4% to $23.3 billion, which topped estimates at $22.8 billion.
Despite strong organic sales growth, core gross margin fell by 150 basis points, primarily due to higher commodity costs, reflecting higher oil prices than a year ago. Nonetheless, its productivity savings program helped improve selling, general, and administrative margins, and operating margin fell 70 basis points to 25.5%.
On the bottom line, the company reported core earnings per share of $2.00, up from $1.99 in the quarter a year ago, and ahead of the consensus at $1.89.
Why the stock soared on the news
P&G maintained its full-year core EPS guidance of $6.89-$7.11, and the company expects headwinds from higher commodity costs and oil prices to increase over the rest of the year.
Nonetheless, the company seemed to reverse earlier concerns about slumping growth, doing so at a time when many consumer brands are struggling. Four percent organic growth is outstanding for any mature consumer staples business, and that's the figure investors should focus on.
The news also came on a day when tech stocks plunged, and the sell-off may have beckoned more investors to rotate into P&G, which is seen as one of the most rock-solid, defensive stocks on the market.
PG Procter & Gamble

Is P&G a buy?
The parent of Tide, Crest, and Pampers is a Dividend King, having increased its dividend for 70 years in a row. It now offers a dividend yield of 2.6%.
Still, P&G stock has been mostly flat over the last five years, and its commentary about increasing headwinds shows that investors should temper their expectations for the rest of the year.
For an investor looking for defensive, dividend-paying stocks or a safe place to ride out the volatility in the AI sector, P&G is a good choice. This administration has imprisoned people in El Salvador and bombed boats suspected of drug smuggling without due process.
The president’s party has abdicated its role as a check on the power of the executive branch.

The president has said unless he wins, the elections are rigged.

I’ve always been more of an anaerobic athlete, meaning I love shorter, faster running and strength workouts. In fact, I love strength so much that even during my first marathon training block, I enthusiastically committed to three heavy lifts a week.
While strength training prevents injuries, makes you more durable, and can even boost your running economy, says Des Clarke, an RRCA-certified run coach based in Phoenix, I often spent evenings in the gym lifting weights instead of allowing my body to recover from 40-mile weeks.
As I started training for a half marathon for the second time, I decided to put more of an emphasis on mileage. I didn’t want to nix strength from my schedule entirely, but I had to figure out how to dial back my time with the weights and increase my running time in a safe, balanced way.
Doing so helped me run a 1:46:50 half marathon on a majorly hilly course. Here’s what I did to get there so you can strike a better balance, too.
How I Increased My Mileage Safely Without Sacrificing Strength
For anyone running half marathons and marathons (especially someone who’s newer to longer distances like I am), higher mileage weeks give you the base you need to run longer and faster.
“If you want to get better at running, it is true that to a point, you need to run more,” says Clarke. “You’re building the aerobic capacity, strength, and durability that you need to run those distances without getting injured.” That looks like building volume incrementally over time, she says.
Before I started half marathon training, I was running at least two times each week for about eight months. I was pretty consistent, but knew I could afford to add more miles. So before starting my plan, I added another day of running to my schedule, and then when I kicked off the first week, I tackled four days a week of running.
I also added some more miles to my midweek runs. Last training cycle, I usually opted for four-milers, but this time, I bumped it up to five or six miles.
Clarke typically recommends repeating the same weekly mileage for two to three weeks in a row to make sure an athlete has adapted to that particular load before increasing again. I did this during several weeks of my plan.
In that same vein, it’s useful to take a deload week every three weeks or so to better absorb training gains, Clarke says. This involves scaling back your mileage by around 10 to 20 percent before returning to your typical volume. My training plan also included these, allowing me recovery time while pushing mileage.
To balance this increase in mileage, I dropped to two lifting days per week instead of three, cutting down on volume (and consequently my overall time spent in the gym), which Clarke recommends. Last year during marathon training, I spent three days a week lifting weights for about an hour or more. This training cycle, I’ve spent 30 to 45 minutes lifting weights one to two times a week. I split up my usual hour-long routine into two separate days and alternated between them.
How Swapping Strength Training for More Miles Paid Off
1. I Actually Felt Recovered Going Into Every Run
I remember how exhausting it felt to spend more than four hours a week strength training on top of 35- to 40-mile weeks during marathon training. Cutting my time in the weight room in half each week (from three hour-long lifts to two 45-minute lifts) not only allowed me to fit in a few extra miles but take my recovery more seriously, too.

The artificial intelligence (AI) investing thesis has been tough during the past month, but a bundle of tech earnings can change sentiment. Alphabet (GOOG -1.08%) (GOOGL -1.24%), Microsoft (MSFT +0.66%), and Amazon (AMZN -0.95%) are some of the tech giants slated to report earnings by the end of the month, and these are the key details every investor should monitor.
AI capital expenditures
If hyperscalers say that they will continue to ramp up spending, it gives chipmakers, neoclouds, and other companies at the center of the AI trade full permission to rebound.
Elon Musk offered some good news when SpaceX (SPCX +1.89%) reported earnings earlier this month. He told investors that hyperscalers and AI enterprises have been relentlessly "hound[ing]" SpaceX for more compute. Even SpaceX is struggling to find compute, with Musk expecting the superintelligence computing capacity shortage to last for years.
That backdrop suggests hyperscalers will spend more than expected and project even higher AI capital expenditures into the fourth quarter and beyond.
That would be good news, but it's equally important to assess how each company will fund its capital expenditures. Microsoft already told investors it would achieve positive free cash flow in its fiscal 2027, suggesting that the AI build-out is sustainable.
Revenue growth rates
All this spending has to translate into positive returns to justify the huge cost of the AI build-out. That's why investors should closely look at year-over-year growth rates for the tech giants. It's already clear that chipmakers are still doing well. Micron (MU +2.46%) posted 379% year-over-year revenue growth in its fiscal Q4 2026 as demand for its memory chips continues to soar.
However, all those chips have to translate into meaningful revenue growth rates for hyperscalers to justify the increased capital expenditures. Alphabet's cloud revenue, specifically, will be on my radar. That part of the business has been accelerating a lot lately, including an 82% year-over-year growth rate in the second quarter. The more Google Cloud's revenue growth rate accelerates in the third quarter, the better it is for the AI trade.

Profitability also matters, but there are two reasons I am not looking at net income as much. First, it's normal for tech innovations to be unprofitable for multiple years before enjoying dramatic profit margin expansion upon profitability. Google Cloud is a great example, since it was unprofitable for more than a decade.
Second, net income has been murky for some tech giants due to their large investments in SpaceX and Anthropic. Returns from those investments influence net income, but don't indicate how well the underlying businesses are actually doing. For this earnings cycle, operating income is a more reliable metric than net income, because the former isn't affected by large investments that are performing well for now.
Forward guidance
Chipmakers have offered forward guidance that implies demand will continue. The projections from tech giants will suggest how they feel about current AI expenditures, and whether it is translating into higher growth rates.
Commentary from tech leaders will also reveal where they see AI heading. For instance, Amazon Chief Executive Officer Andy Jassy told investors that Amazon Web Services was booming in Q2, and that "there's a lot to be excited about."

The $500 Billion Question: Can Google Cloud’s Massive AI Backlog Outrun Its Mind-Boggling CapEx Boom on Oct. 28?
Google Cloud's backlog just crossed $500 billion while free cash flow turned negative for the first time ever, and Wednesday's earnings report will reveal whether Alphabet's historic spending spree is pulling ahead of its own ability to pay for it.
Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL | GOOGL Price Prediction, NASDAQ:GOOG) reports third-quarter results after the close on Wednesday, October 28. Google Cloud’s backlog stands at $514 billion, and 2026 CapEx guidance runs $195 billion to $205 billion. This report shows which one is growing faster.
Record Cloud Growth Meets Negative Free Cash Flow
Last quarter, revenue rose 24.2% to $119.80 billion, ahead of the $116.91 billion consensus. Google Cloud led again. Revenue there rose 82% to $24.77 billion, speeding up from 63% in Q1 and 34% a year ago, while Cloud operating margin expanded to 35.6% from 20.7%.
Costs grew just as fast. CapEx rose 100% to $44.92 billion, free cash flow came in at negative $5.86 billion — the first time ever — and management raised its 2026 CapEx range from $180 billion to $190 billion. To pay for it, Alphabet raised about $70 billion in equity and debt and suspended buybacks.
Reported EPS of $9.11 included a $99.03 billion equity securities gain, yet shares fell 6.89% on the day of the report. GOOG closed Friday at $317.28, down 5.83% over the past week.
Consensus Calls for Nearly 25% Revenue Growth
The full-year EPS figure includes the first half’s equity gains, which makes the quarterly estimate the cleaner gauge of operating profit.
Backlog Conversion and Margins Will Set the Tone
My first focus will be the backlog. It rose by more than $50 billion sequentially last quarter, and management expects to recognize just over 50% of it within 24 months. Sundar Pichai said in July, “We are still in a supply-constrained environment.”
Margins come next. Alphabet planned to lean on third-party capacity in Q3 as a bridge, which management said would create “modest margin pressure,” on top of Wiz integration costs and rising depreciation. You should compare Cloud margin against 35.6% and consolidated operating margin against 34%.
On spending, any change to the 2026 range matters, as does early color on 2027, when management expects CapEx to “increase significantly.” TPU system sales add another variable. That revenue ramps as Alphabet leaves 2026, with the “vast majority” arriving in 2027.
All that CapEx has to be powered, cooled, and connected by somebody, which is the entire point of a free report we put together on seven AI infrastructure suppliers that aren’t the chipmakers: you can grab it here.
Search still has to fund the expansion. Revenue there grew 17% to $63.3 billion, and AI Mode passed 1 billion monthly users. A court has already rejected a forced breakup of Google’s ad-tech business, so any detail on the remaining behavioral remedies could also move opinion.
A $514 Billion Backlog Has to Turn Into Cash
Alphabet beat estimates in all 8 of its last reports. Even so, the stock’s moves on report day ranged from a 9.97% gain to a 6.89% drop, and the market now cares most about how efficiently that capital gets spent. If the backlog turns into revenue fast enough to steady free cash flow while CapEx keeps rising, the spending case gets easier to defend heading into a greater 2027.

Former CEO of Alphabet Inc.'s Google, Eric Schmidt, said China trails the U.S. in the AI race by roughly six months, but it could still be the winner.
In a podcast called In Good Company, hosted by Nicolai Tangen, CEO of Norges Bank Investment Management, on Wednesday, Schmidt said, "I don't know that they will get ahead, but I will tell you that…if they're six months behind, then we're already losing because their strategy is that the products are free."
Chinese AI models are often free or less expensive, potentially attracting consumers in developing economies that cannot afford costly, closed Western systems, he said. Open-weight models could further accelerate global use.
He credited China's progress partly to access to advanced chips he said were "not supposed to have" and were "pilfered or smuggled" into the country. He also cited distillation, in which developers query Western AI systems and train their own models using the responses.
Schmidt, who personally owns a stake in Anthropic, rejected comparisons between the AI industry and a speculative bubble. He pointed to Anthropic's revenue growth and paying customers as evidence of commercial demand. Schmidt said that Google set a revenue-growth record during his tenure as CEO, but Anthropic surpassed it by growing at more than twice the pace.
"That's real growth. It's not fake. It's real money, with real customers who are paying for something useful," he said.
AI's Price Tag: A Risk for US Big Tech?
Schmidt echoed IMD Business School professor Howard Yu, who told Benzinga that OpenAI and Anthropic's four-to-six-month lead over Chinese AI rivals could prove "very perishable," as many users do not need the most advanced models.
He cited Tencent Holdings Ltd's WeChat agent, which quickly generated personalized guidance by scanning medicine packaging, to illustrate how less sophisticated AI can deliver practical value. For businesses, he added, cost matters, with executives weighing AI spending against hiring more employees.
In June, Polsia AI CEO Ben Cera warned that cheaper Chinese open-source AI models like DeepSeek's R-1 model and Alibaba Group Holdings' Qwen3 and Qwen2.5 could undermine the business models and valuations of OpenAI and Anthropic by offering near-frontier capabilities at a fraction of the cost.
He argued that enterprises may no longer justify spending millions on AI when comparable alternatives cost far less, declaring, "The bubble isn't AI. It's the price of AI." Cera added that AI model-focused companies could face the biggest losses, while hyperscalers such as Alphabet may be better positioned to weather the shift.

JPMorgan's shift in tone is remarkable given the longstanding skepticism toward digital assets from its CEO Jamie Dimon. In 2017, he derided Bitcoin as a "fraud" heading toward a crash. He has kept up a barrage of criticism against Bitcoin, dismissing it as "a pet rock" and "worthless" over the years. Just last year, JPMorgan began allowing its clients to buy Bitcoin as banks developed a stronger interest in crypto.
"I don't think you should smoke, but I defend your right to smoke," Dimon said during JPMorgan's annual investor day in May 2025. "I defend your right to buy bitcoin."
However, the report offered a significant caveat for its projection: It still doesn't recommend Bitcoin as something that investors should purchase for a diversified portfolio.
Diving into JPMorgan's Bitcoin forecast
Bitcoin is a digital asset designed to be sent electronically between users anywhere in the world without a bank or government facilitating the transfer. Therefore, its value is not determined by a central government. It only stems from what an investor is prepared to pay. Bitcoin's volatility made JPMorgan analysts cautious about incorporating it in investment portfolios.
"At the moment, we do not make a case for bitcoin (BTC) as a diversifier in portfolios due to its unstable market correlations," JPMorgan analysts Sheena Shah and Dennis Cristallo wrote in the analysis. "We see bitcoin as a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing."

4 California billionaires saw their wealth soar 322% over the past two years — but paid 0.04% a year in state income tax
California, like most states, taxes the wages people earn from their jobs. But in 2019, 2020 and 2023, Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin each owed California just 13.3 cents in income tax on what they got from Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL), according to estimates from three economists.
That's because Alphabet paid the 53-year-olds $1 each in those years. Neither reported selling Alphabet stock, and the company didn't pay dividends until 2024.

The figures come from a working paper by economists Jasper Boll, Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, who work at the University of California, Berkeley, and the Paris School of Economics.
The National Bureau of Economic Research, a nonprofit research group in Cambridge, Massachusetts, released it in May and most recently revised it in August. Like other NBER working papers, it hasn't been peer-reviewed.
The economists went through Securities and Exchange Commission filings on the four billionaires they count as California residents. Besides Page and Brin, that's Meta (NASDAQ:META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg, 42, and Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang, 63.
By the end of 2025, the four were worth a combined $882 billion, up from $209 billion three years earlier. The authors link that 322% jump to the AI boom and the run-up in Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia shares. But over the same three years, their California income tax tied to that stock averaged about 0.04% of its value a year.
Why California's income tax barely touches billionaire wealth
On November 3, California voters decide on Proposition 40, which would charge a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires who lived in the state January 1, 2026. They could spread the payments over five years, and most of the money would go to healthcare to help make up for federal Medicaid cuts passed in July 2025. California isn't the only state looking at new taxes on the very rich.
Saez says in the paper that he advised on how the measure was written and how much it would raise, and that he wasn't paid for it.

A procurement officer sits down on a Monday morning to build a budget for an enterprise AI agent rollout. They open eight browser tabs, one for each of the primary platforms: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, xAI, Meta, ServiceNow, and Salesforce. The goal is simple — find a per-seat or per-unit price to drop into a spreadsheet. By the time they reach the end of the list, no single metric has appeared that lets them compare one agent against another. What they have instead is a row of quote-gated portals, usage meters and third-party estimates: enough material to fill the spreadsheet, not enough to defend it.
Four of the eight publish no public enterprise-agent price on their own surface. OpenAI Presence lists no price on its product page or its announcement; the service is not self-serve, is limited to eligible enterprise customers, and routes buyers to contact sales or an account team — a quote-gated enterprise SKU, where the pricing mechanism exists and simply is not shown. Meta's Business Agent announcement says getting started is free and that paid subscription offerings are planned, but publishes no seat or subscription price. Meta's own developer documentation — which returned a 400 on direct fetch and reached us through an indexed snippet plus two independent third-party guides — carries the one Meta number that exists: $2.00 per 1 million tokens for Business Agent replies on the WhatsApp Business Platform, effective August 1, roughly four to five cents a message. The enterprise custom-agent platform stays unpublished. ServiceNow's AI agents page carries a "Contact us for a quote" call to action and the site has no official pricing page at all; third-party estimates put ITSM at $70 to $200+ per fulfiller per month, which are not ServiceNow figures. Google Gemini Enterprise closes the four: its official pricing surfaces display no per-seat dollar rate, and the $21-to-$60 range in circulation is third-party reported US list pricing, never confirmed on a current Google page.
The two that do publish hand you units that refuse to line up. Microsoft Copilot Studio sells a capacity pack of 25,000 Copilot Credits at $200.00 a month off a published rate card, alongside a pay-as-you-go meter through Azure. Microsoft has moved off the older model in which 25,000 messages cost $200, and because consumption now depends on how an agent is designed and used, a message no longer maps to a flat price. Salesforce Agentforce, whose pricing page was last modified October 19, publishes the fullest card in the group — Flex Credits at $500 per 100,000 credits with each Agentforce action drawing 20 of them, a $5 per-user license, a $125 add-on, a $150 industry add-on, a $50 Coworker license, a Max Edition from $550 — all of it off that page. It also shows $2 per conversation, except the card carrying that price now reads, to anyone arriving as a new buyer, "For existing Agentforce Conversations customers. Contact your Account Executive for more information." A published price, retired inside the page that still prints it. Credits, conversations, actions and seats do not convert into one another, which is why two vendors with honest rate cards still cannot be ranked against each other from public information — the problem four rival agents and the infrastructure pricing gap both already set

Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs has cut its 12-month target for South Korea's Kospi Index by 25%, citing mounting concerns over artificial intelligence investments and more conservative equity valuations.
Strategists led by Timothy Moe lowered their target to 9,000 from 12,000 after the benchmark plunged more than 35% from its June peak.
Despite the downgrade, the revised forecast still implies upside of more than 60% from current levels, reflecting the bank's view that Korean equities have become significantly undervalued.
The investment bank had previously raised its Kospi target in June and maintained its bullish outlook even as global technology stocks began retreating amid concerns about AI spending.
South Korea's market has been particularly vulnerable because of its heavy exposure to semiconductor manufacturers Samsung Electronics (KRX:005930) and SK Hynix (KRX:000660).
Both companies have benefited from demand for memory chips used in AI infrastructure, making the Kospi a major indicator of investor sentiment toward the technology.
However, concerns about rising financing costs, massive infrastructure investments and uncertain returns have triggered widespread selling across Korean equities.
Goldman's strategists said the market was pricing in an excessively pessimistic outlook for corporate fundamentals.
The Kospi's 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratio has fallen to approximately four, a level not seen across 18 major markets since 2006.
Korean stocks now trade at roughly half the valuation of Indonesian equities, highlighting the scale of the recent selloff.
According to the bank's estimates, current semiconductor valuations imply a 65% decline in sector earnings in 2027, a scenario the strategists consider overly pessimistic.
Meanwhile, companies outside the memory chip sector, representing approximately half the Kospi, trade at 7.6 times forward earnings.
Despite lowering its overall market target, Goldman continues to favour opportunities in power, industrials, corporate governance-related stocks, and companies benefiting from domestic economic recovery and Korean popular culture.
